content_html:
Reversible, gradient-free weight editing for local language models on CPU, Apple Silicon and CUDA.

v0.1.0. W-ISA provides a JSON instruction format, a compiler and a Python runtime for named weight operations, request-scoped patches and snapshot restoration. The repository includes executable experiments and their recorded measurements.

Compile a small JSON program, bind it to PyTorch parameter names, and change live weights with deterministic linear algebra. The runtime freezes the model and performs edits under torch.no_grad().

The default loader targets Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct. It also accepts a local checkpoint path or another Transformers causal LM, including HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM-135M-Instruct. Parameter names and dimensions come from the loaded model.

Papers and citation

Both papers are by Ekrem Aksoy and are available on arXiv:

Paper Read DOI
W-ISA: Transactional Execution of Weight-Space Intervention Programs arXiv:2611.13232 · PDF 10.48550/arXiv.2611.13232
NCP: Verifier-Guided Optimization of Weight-Space Control Policies arXiv:2611.13236 · PDF 10.48550/arXiv.2611.13236

Research context and attribution

We credit Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab for the weight-space programming perspective presented in Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights (November 2, 2026). Their article explores LLM-native weight inspection and editing. W-ISA develops a structured instruction runtime with validation, request scopes and restoration around weight interventions.

Related foundations include Elhage et al.'s A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits for head and residual-stream structure, and Arditi et al.'s Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction for directional behavioral interventions. Both are referenced in the article above. The article also links Tracr: Compiled Transformers as a Laboratory for Interpretability, which compiles programs into transformer models. W-ISA compiles intervention instructions for the parameters of an existing model.

Run it

From a checkout, create a virtual environment and install the package:

python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install -e .
.venv/bin/wisa demo

Installation downloads dependencies. The self-contained demo changes a fixed matrix's output from [5, 11] to approximately [3, -1], then restores [5, 11] exactly.

Python 3.10+ is declared; the tested interpreter is Python 3.12.9. Direct runtime dependencies are torch, transformers, and numpy, plus their normal transitive packages.

Inspect a cached model with .venv/bin/wisa inspect --local-files-only --contains mlp.down_proj. Use --model /path/to/checkpoint for a local checkpoint. Omitting --local-files-only allows Transformers to download public model files from Hugging Face; generation runs locally.

For a before/edit/after/undo comparison on cached Qwen weights:

.venv/bin/wisa run --local-files-only --program examples/prune.json --prompt "What is a matrix?" --max-new-tokens 32 --undo

Run .venv/bin/python examples/roundtrip.py for the pretrained SmolLM experiment. The first run downloads the model when needed; subsequent runs can use --local-files-only. All model-running commands accept --device.

The pruning example zeros small values in Qwen's first MLP down-projection. Inspect parameter names before using the example with a different architecture. CLI edits operate on in-memory weights for the current process. For an application that keeps a model resident, use WeightRuntime directly.

--device auto selects CUDA, then MPS, then CPU according to PyTorch availability. Use --device cuda for the current CUDA device or --device cuda:1 for an indexed device. --device mps and --device cpu select those backends explicitly. The loader checks availability and CUDA indices before loading model files. Weights default to FP32; --dtype float16 and --dtype bfloat16 select the other supported model dtypes.

For NVIDIA GPUs, install the CUDA-enabled PyTorch build for your platform using the PyTorch installation selector, then install W-ISA. Run .venv/bin/wisa inspect --device cuda --contains mlp.down_proj to inspect a model, or .venv/bin/python examples/roundtrip.py --device cuda --output artifacts/cuda-roundtrip.json for the head-ablation and projection experiment. Its report records the selected device, arithmetic dtype, weight changes, undo and replay results.

Instructions

Source contains "version": 1 and an "instructions" array. Each instruction has op and target; the target is a full name from model.named_parameters(). Operand fields refer to named arrays in an NPZ file supplied by --operands, or to a mapping of numeric arrays/tensors passed to compile_program().

For a matrix $W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$:

Opcode Extra fields Operation
ADD delta, optional alpha=1 $W\leftarrow W+\alpha D$; exactly matching shape
SCALE factor $W\leftarrow fW$
RANK1 left, right, optional alpha=1 $W\leftarrow W+\alpha uv^T$, with $u\in\mathbb{R}^m$, $v\in\mathbb{R}^n$
PROJECT_OUT direction $W\leftarrow W-(W\hat v)\hat v^T$, with $\hat v=v/\lVert v\rVert_2$
WRITE_KEY key, value $W\leftarrow W+(y-Wk)k^T/(k^Tk)$
PRUNE threshold Set entries with $

ADD, SCALE, and PRUNE also work on vectors and other dense floating-point parameter shapes. The rank-one and projection instructions require matrices because their operands describe matrix input/output spaces. Thresholds are nonnegative. The compiler checks parameter names, operand shapes, finite values, instruction fields and nonzero projection directions before writing weights. NPZ loading uses allow_pickle=False.

Every instruction also accepts an optional slice array, one entry per parameter dimension. null selects that entire axis; [start, stop] selects a nonempty, zero-based, half-open range within the axis. For example, "slice": [null, [0, 64]] selects the first 64 columns of a matrix while preserving the other columns. Operand shapes are checked against the selected region. With no slice, the instruction retains its original whole-parameter behavior. Reports count changed entries and the delta norm in the selected region; entries outside it have zero delta. Backups still cover the whole target parameter, and overlapping slices execute in source order.

PROJECT_OUT removes an input direction, so $W'v\approx0$. WRITE_KEY gives $W'k\approx y$ and preserves the response to vectors orthogonal to $k$. It is the minimum-Frobenius-norm single-key correction in exact arithmetic. For a biased linear layer, pass the desired pre-bias output as value.

For the demo, $W=[[1,2],[3,4]]$, $k=[1,2]$, and $y=[3,-1]$ give $W'=[[0.6,1.2],[0.6,-0.8]]$. The output changes from $[5,11]$ to approximately $[3,-1]$; undo restores $[5,11]$ exactly.

Embedding the runtime

Import compile_program and WeightRuntime from wisa. Construct a runtime with your model, compile a source mapping against that model and an operand mapping, then pass the returned Program to runtime.execute(program). runtime.undo() restores the last successful nonempty program. runtime.discard_undo() releases its saved tensors without changing weights.

The compiler produces a tuple of bound instructions and detached CPU FP64 operand copies. A compiled program owns its operand copies. The compiled IR contains PyTorch tensors. The runtime rechecks target names and shapes before writing. The model adapter handles local loading, chat templates, and greedy generation.

Execution preserves Parameter identity, including ordinary tied embedding/LM head weights. Instructions run in source order; each result is rounded to the parameter's original dtype before the next instruction reads it. Reports contain the norm and number of actually changed entries after that rounding.

All edited targets are backed up before the first write. An execution exception or cancellation restores those backups and keeps the preceding undo point. Successful execution replaces the undo point; an empty program preserves it. Undo restores the saved parameter values. Before restoration, the runtime checks parameter identity, shape and dtype against the snapshot.

runtime.temporary(program) adds an owned request scope: it holds the model's reentrant lock, applies the program, and restores the entry state in finally. Nested scopes and additional runtime execute()/undo() calls are tracked; the preceding public undo point survives the scope. Runtime instances wrapping the same model object share this lock and snapshot state. This includes no-match requests in the controller. Coordination is keyed by the model object and covers operations routed through the shared runtime lock.

Use runtime.lock around other inference calls sharing that model. After a weight change, start generation with a fresh KV cache, as the CLI and controller do. Scope cleanup runs through Python's finally mechanism.

Numerical behavior and cost

The model stays on its CPU, MPS or CUDA device while edits are calculated on CPU in FP64. Host transfer and dtype conversion are separate operations. Results are checked for finite values, rounded to the original weight dtype and copied back into the existing parameter view. The runtime synchronizes each touched accelerator before snapshots and after writes; restoration also waits for pending device work. CUDA synchronization uses the actual device index of each parameter.

The arithmetic is deterministic for fixed inputs and execution settings. Reports measure the changes after rounding to the model's dtype. The recorded CPU/MPS tests compare weights bit for bit; generation uses greedy decoding.

Every matrix instruction takes $O(mn)$ arithmetic for the selected region, including the rank-one ones: this implementation materializes that region's updated dense matrix. Projection uses vector products and an outer product. For instructions selecting $N_j$ elements each, execution costs $O(P+B+\sum_j N_j+A)$, where $P$ is the number of named parameters inspected, $B$ is the total element count of full target parameters backed up once, and $A$ counts operand elements checked. Host/device transfers include both full target backups and per-instruction selected regions.

Beyond model storage, peak memory includes the previous undo snapshot, the new transaction backups, compiled FP64 operands, and a constant number of dense FP64 work buffers for the largest target. Backups use the original weight dtype on CPU. Snapshots copy the targeted parameters. During normal idle operation, one undo snapshot remains resident. FP32 Qwen 0.5B weights alone are roughly 2 GB; inference activations, caches, and edit workspaces add to that.

Validation

Use the VS Code task W-ISA: offline tests, or run PYTHONPATH=src HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 TRANSFORMERS_OFFLINE=1 .venv/bin/python -m unittest discover -s tests -v. The tests use unittest, fixed matrices, and a tiny randomly initialized Qwen2ForCausalLM. For debugging, place a breakpoint in the runtime and launch the wisa module with the demo argument using the workspace virtual environment.

The November 4, 2026 run used ARM64 macOS, Python 3.12.9, PyTorch 2.15.0, Transformers 5.22.1 and NumPy 2.5.4: 66 tests passed in the CPU/MPS environment. Coverage includes independent NumPy/hand-derived answers, extreme direction scales, rounding, rollback after partial execution, tied parameters, repeated execution, MPS operands, all opcodes on CPU/MPS, and Qwen logit changes with exact undo/replay. Seven additional slice tests cover head-only ablation, noncontiguous MPS writes, operand shape checks, overlapping slices, rollback, projection, and invalid bounds. New evaluation/profile/control tests cover token accounting, paired activation means, threshold calibration, nested request scopes, cancellation during writes, multiple runtime instances, rule ordering, operand snapshots, and streaming close. Dependency checks and the installed CLI demo passed. The loader uses the torch_dtype argument shared with the declared Transformers 4.x range.

The tiny Qwen checkpoint loader test uses real locally saved weights and a mocked tokenizer loader. The separate experiment below exercised real pretrained SmolLM weights, its tokenizer and chat template, and MPS generation. The weights were downloaded from Hugging Face; all inference was local.

CUDA tests cover opcode parity, FP32/FP16/BF16 rounding, sliced writes, rollback, request cancellation, stream completion, indexed devices and tiny-Qwen inference. Hardware cases are enabled by torch.cuda.is_available() and device count. Device selection and synchronization routing also have mocked backend tests.

Pretrained SmolLM roundtrip

Run .venv/bin/python examples/roundtrip.py --local-files-only to reproduce the experiment using the cached model. The runner accepts --model, --device, --layer-index, --head-index, repeatable --prompt, and --max-new-tokens options. Defaults use the tenth transformer block (layers[9]), query head 0, and four fixed prompts with greedy decoding.

SCALE with factor 0 zeros only o_proj.weight[:, 0:64]. With nine query heads of dimension 64, these columns carry head 0's contribution to the residual stream. Other heads' columns, and the shared GQA key/value projections, remain unchanged. This is output ablation: attention computation runs and the selected head's output contribution is zeroed.

PROJECT_OUT edits that block's MLP down-projection. Its fixed direction comes from the measured down-projection input at the last token of the first prompt, before either edit. The roundtrip measures the two operations together.

Two separate process runs matched exactly on saved logits, token sequences, measured direction, and model-weight hashes. Within each process, the runner checks baseline repeat, edited repeat, undo, and replay. All four prompts changed logits; three changed their generated token sequences. Direction response norm fell from 6.4653542 to $1.4276433\times10^{-7}$. Edit transactions took 9.2–14.6 ms across the four measured executions, excluding model loading and inference.

See the measured results, first JSON report, and independent process report. The runner also saves raw FP32 logits, the measured FP64 operand, and the exact JSON program, together with the model revision and execution environment.

Qwen2.5-1.5B execution comparison

The rank-one benchmark compares original inference, scoped W-ISA materialization, and a PyTorch forward hook computing the equivalent linear update. The recorded run uses FP32 MPS weights, layer 9's 1536×8960 MLP down-projection, and normalized sine/cosine vectors with strength 0.1. A 51-token prompt is decoded for fixed 32-, 128-, and 512-token budgets, including EOS. Each mode/length has one warm-up and five timed requests; mode order rotates between repetitions and every token step is synchronized.

Reproduce the two Qwen experiments with the cached checkpoint:

HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 TRANSFORMERS_OFFLINE=1 .venv/bin/python examples/roundtrip.py \
	--model Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct --device mps --max-new-tokens 48 \
	--local-files-only --output artifacts/qwen15b-roundtrip.json
HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1 TRANSFORMERS_OFFLINE=1 .venv/bin/python examples/intervention_benchmark.py \
	--model Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct --device mps --dtype float32 \
	--lengths 32 128 512 --warmups 1 --repeats 5 --local-files-only \
	--output artifacts/qwen15b-benchmark.json

For an initial model download, omit the offline environment settings and --local-files-only. The benchmark accepts caller-selected model, module, device, dtype, prompt, intervention strength and token budgets.

Generated tokens Original request (s) W-ISA request (s) Hook request (s)
32 1.1858 1.2312 1.1868
128 4.7445 4.8527 4.7873
512 18.7117 19.3735 19.4961

Values are medians of five complete requests, including setup and restoration. The graph shows medians and interquartile ranges. All three modes returned identical token sequences at every measured length. Hook versus materialized prompt logits differed by at most 0.000184; the materialized weights matched the rounded NumPy reference exactly. The intervention changed baseline prompt logits by up to 0.041107.

One target snapshot occupies 52.5 MiB and one full FP64 buffer occupies 105 MiB. The maximum sampled RSS increase during a W-ISA request was 498.94 MiB, with 10 ms sampling. RSS and MPS allocator counters are recorded separately because they overlap in unified-memory accounting. The raw JSON retains all 45 requests, setup/restore times, TTFT, decode times and memory counters. The CSV tabulates the timing measurements. The runner exports SVG and PGFPlots source; the compiled figure is also included.

The separate head/projection roundtrip changed all four prompt-logit distributions and three generated sequences. Projection residual was $2.52421\times10^{-8}$ relative to its original response. Undo and replay checks matched the recorded weights, logits and token sequences.

Evaluation, profiles, and match-action

The control-plane report records full WikiText-2 measurements, held-out contrastive-profile results, and real MPS request-isolation tests. The combined original ablation raised perplexity by 0.3754%. A separate formal-minus-casual direction raised it by 0.0040%. The controller gated four of twelve held-out requests: four logit distributions changed and all twelve greedy token sequences were preserved. The report includes completion-preference scores, trigger counts and generated text.

perplexity(model, token_ids, context_length, stride) computes token-weighted NLL. It scores every token except the first exactly once and returns window-level losses, counts, protocol settings, and elapsed time. The four-condition runner compares original weights, head-only ablation, MLP-only projection, and their combination on identical tokens.

ActivationProfiler(runtime, tokenizer, ActivationSite(...)) captures an input or output activation at a named module with last-token or mean-token pooling. contrast(positive, negative) returns detached CPU FP64 class means and their difference, plus source metadata. profile.operands("v_diff") feeds the compiler directly; profile.save(...) stores numeric NPZ arrays and JSON provenance. The style example uses disjoint topic sets for profiling, threshold calibration, and evaluation. It also saves a symbolic PROJECT_OUT program. Each profile records its capture location and feature space.

Rule(name, site, direction, threshold, program) defines one match-action row. MatchActionController(runtime, tokenizer, rules) uses caller-supplied rule order: the first rule with cosine_score > threshold wins. All scores are measured before any patch; identical sites share an activation capture. Rule tensors are copied on registration. Threshold calibration is a separate function operating on the designated calibration set.

controller.generate(prompt) wraps local greedy generation. For other synchronous inference engines, use controller.run(prompt, callback) or hold controller.session(prompt) for the full inference lifetime. The result separates inference time from control time, including restoration and any lock wait. These APIs serialize requests sharing one mutable model.

controller.stream(prompt, iterator_factory) keeps the scope open while consuming a synchronous iterator. Close the returned generator on early disconnect, using the same thread, for example through contextlib.closing. The controller owns cleanup of the supplied iterator. For an async server, run the entire synchronous request in a worker rather than holding a thread-owned RLock across arbitrary await points. The API runs inside the caller's Python application.

To reproduce the measurements, run the following from the workspace:

  • .venv/bin/python examples/fetch_wikitext.py downloads the public test corpus once, using the standard library. See data attribution.
  • .venv/bin/python examples/perplexity.py evaluates the complete cached split. --max-tokens explicitly selects a shorter pilot; the report marks whether the full test split was evaluated.
  • .venv/bin/python examples/profile_style.py --corpus data/wikitext2-test.json extracts the profile, evaluates held-out behavior, and measures its corpus cost.
  • .venv/bin/python examples/match_action.py checks calibrated gating, exact undo/repeat, failure injection, stream closure, and two threaded requests.

Model-running examples use cached checkpoints; the roundtrip example also supports initial model download. Runtime dependencies are torch, transformers and numpy.

See CONTRIBUTING.md for test and experiment conventions and SECURITY.md for the trust boundary. The GitHub workflow runs CPU tests against an installed wheel. The linked experiment reports record local MPS measurements and their execution environment.

For instructions selecting $N_j$ elements each, execution costs $O(P+B+\sum_j N_j+A)$, where $P$ is the number of named parameters inspected, $B$ is the total element count of full target parameters backed up once, and $A$ counts operand elements checked. Host/device transfers include both full target backups and per-instruction selected regions. Beyond model storage, peak memory includes the previous undo snapshot, the new transaction backups, compiled FP64 operands, and a constant number of dense FP64 work buffers for the largest target. Backups use the original weight dtype on CPU. Snapshots copy the targeted parameters. During normal idle operation, one undo snapshot remains resident. FP32 Qwen 0.5B weights alone are roughly 2 GB; inference activations, caches, and edit workspaces add to that. content_html_zh:
Reversible, gradient-free weight editing for local language models on CPU, Apple Silicon and CUDA.

v0.1.0. W-ISA provides a JSON instruction format, a compiler and a Python runtime for named weight operations, request-scoped patches and snapshot restoration. The repository includes executable experiments and their recorded measurements.

Compile a small JSON program, bind it to PyTorch parameter names, and change live weights with deterministic linear algebra. The runtime freezes the model and performs edits under torch.no_grad().

The default loader targets Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct. It also accepts a local checkpoint path or another Transformers causal LM, including HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM-135M-Instruct. Parameter names and dimensions come from the loaded model.

Papers and citation

Both papers are by Ekrem Aksoy and are available on arXiv:

Paper Read DOI
W-ISA: Transactional Execution of Weight-Space Intervention Programs arXiv:2611.13232 · PDF 10.48550/arXiv.2611.13232

Research context and attribution

We credit Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab for the weight-space programming perspective presented in Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights (November 2, 2026). Their article explores LLM-native weight inspection and editing. W-ISA develops a structured instruction runtime with validation, request scopes and restoration around weight interventions.

Related foundations include Elhage et al.'s A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits for head and residual-stream structure, and Arditi et al.'s Refusal in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction for directional behavioral interventions. Both are referenced in the article above. The article also links Tracr: Compiled Transformers as a Laboratory for Interpretability, which compiles programs into transformer models. W-ISA compiles intervention instructions for the parameters of an existing model.

Run it

From a checkout, create a virtual environment and install the package:

python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install -e .
.venv/bin/wisa demo

Installation downloads dependencies. The self-contained demo changes a fixed matrix's output from [5, 11] to approximately [3, -1], then restores [5, 11] exactly.

Python 3.10+ is declared; the tested interpreter is Python 3.12.9. Direct runtime dependencies are torch, transformers, and numpy, plus their normal transitive packages.

Inspect a cached model with .venv/bin/wisa inspect --local-files-only --contains mlp.down_proj. Use --model /path/to/checkpoint for a local checkpoint. Omitting --local-files-only allows Transformers to download public model files from Hugging Face; generation runs locally.

For a before/edit/after/undo comparison on cached Qwen weights:

.venv/bin/wisa run --local-files-only --program examples/prune.json --prompt "What is a matrix?" --max-new-tokens 32 --undo

Run .venv/bin/python examples/roundtrip.py for the pretrained SmolLM experiment. The first run downloads the model when needed; subsequent runs can use --local-files-only. All model-running commands accept --device.

The pruning example zeros small values in Qwen's first MLP down-projection. Inspect parameter names before using the example with a different architecture. CLI edits operate on in-memory weights for the current process. For an application that keeps a model resident, use WeightRuntime directly.

--device auto selects CUDA, then MPS, then CPU according to PyTorch availability. Use --device cuda for the current CUDA device or --device cuda:1 for an indexed device. --device mps and --device cpu select those backends explicitly. The loader checks availability and CUDA indices before loading model files. Weights default to FP32; --dtype float16 and --dtype bfloat16 select the other supported model dtypes.

For NVIDIA GPUs, install the CUDA-enabled PyTorch build for your platform using the PyTorch installation selector, then install W-ISA. Run .venv/bin/wisa inspect --device cuda --contains mlp.down_proj to inspect a model, or .venv/bin/python examples/roundtrip.py --device cuda --output artifacts/cuda-roundtrip.json for the head-ablation and projection experiment. Its report records the selected device, arithmetic dtype, weight changes, undo and replay results.

指示

Source contains "version": 1 and an "instructions" array. Each instruction has op and target; the target is a full name from model.named_parameters(). Operand fields refer to named arrays in an NPZ file supplied by --operands, or to a mapping of numeric arrays/tensors passed to compile_program().

For a matrix $W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$:

Opcode Extra fields 手术
ADD delta, optional alpha=1 $W\leftarrow W+\alpha D$; exactly matching shape
SCALE factor $W\leftarrow fW$
RANK1 left, right, optional alpha=1 $W\leftarrow W+\alpha uv^T$, with $u\in\mathbb{R}^m$, $v\in\mathbb{R}^n$
PROJECT_OUT 方向 $W\leftarrow W-(W\hat v)\hat v^T$, with $\hat v=v/\lVert v\rVert_2$
WRITE_KEY key, value $W\leftarrow W+(y-Wk)k^T/(k^Tk)$
PRUNE 临界点 Set entries with $

ADD, SCALE, and PRUNE also work on vectors and other dense floating-point parameter shapes. The rank-one and projection instructions require matrices because their operands describe matrix input/output spaces. Thresholds are nonnegative. The compiler checks parameter names, operand shapes, finite values, instruction fields and nonzero projection directions before writing weights. NPZ loading uses allow_pickle=False.

Every instruction also accepts an optional slice array, one entry per parameter dimension. null selects that entire axis; [start, stop] selects a nonempty, zero-based, half-open range within the axis. For example, "slice": [null, [0, 64]] selects the first 64 columns of a matrix while preserving the other columns. Operand shapes are checked against the selected region. With no slice, the instruction retains its original whole-parameter behavior. Reports count changed entries and the delta norm in the selected region; entries outside it have zero delta. Backups still cover the whole target parameter, and overlapping slices execute in source order.

PROJECT_OUT removes an input direction, so $W'v\approx0$. WRITE_KEY gives $W'k\approx y$ and preserves the response to vectors orthogonal to $k$. It is the minimum-Frobenius-norm single-key correction in exact arithmetic. For a biased linear layer, pass the desired pre-bias output as value.

For the demo, $W=[[1,2],[3,4]]$, $k=[1,2]$, and $y=[3,-1]$ give $W'=[[0.6,1.2],[0.6,-0.8]]$. The output changes from $[5,11]$ to approximately $[3,-1]$; undo restores $[5,11]$ exactly.

Embedding the runtime

Import compile_program and WeightRuntime from wisa. Construct a runtime with your model, compile a source mapping against that model and an operand mapping, then pass the returned Program to runtime.execute(program). runtime.undo() restores the last successful nonempty program. runtime.discard_undo() releases its saved tensors without changing weights.

The compiler produces a tuple of bound instructions and detached CPU FP64 operand copies. A compiled program owns its operand copies. The compiled IR contains PyTorch tensors. The runtime rechecks target names and shapes before writing. The model adapter handles local loading, chat templates, and greedy generation.

Execution preserves Parameter identity, including ordinary tied embedding/LM head weights. Instructions run in source order; each result is rounded to the parameter's original dtype before the next instruction reads it. Reports contain the norm and number of actually changed entries after that rounding.

All edited targets are backed up before the first write. An execution exception or cancellation restores those backups and keeps the preceding undo point. Successful execution replaces the undo point; an empty program preserves it. Undo restores the saved parameter values. Before restoration, the runtime checks parameter identity, shape and dtype against the snapshot.

runtime.temporary(program) adds an owned request scope: it holds the model's reentrant lock, applies the program, and restores the entry state in finally. Nested scopes and additional runtime execute()/undo() calls are tracked; the preceding public undo point survives the scope. Runtime instances wrapping the same model object share this lock and snapshot state. This includes no-match requests in the controller. Coordination is keyed by the model object and covers operations routed through the shared runtime lock.

Numerical behavior and cost

The model stays on its CPU, MPS or CUDA device while edits are calculated on CPU in FP64. Host transfer and dtype conversion are separate operations. Results are checked for finite values, rounded to the original weight dtype and copied back into the existing parameter view. The runtime synchronizes each touched accelerator before snapshots and after writes; restoration also waits for pending device work. CUDA synchronization uses the actual device index of each parameter.

The arithmetic is deterministic for fixed inputs and execution settings. Reports measure the changes after rounding to the model's dtype. The recorded CPU/MPS tests compare weights bit for bit; generation uses greedy decoding.

Every matrix instruction takes $O(mn)$ arithmetic for the selected region, including the rank-one ones: this implementation materializes that region's updated dense matrix. Projection uses vector products and an outer product. For instructions selecting $N_j$ elements each, execution costs $O(P+B+\sum_j N_j+A)$, where $P$ is the number of named parameters inspected, $B$ is the total element count of full target parameters backed up once, and $A$ counts operand elements checked. Host/device transfers include both full target backups and per-instruction selected regions.

Beyond model storage, peak memory includes the previous undo snapshot, the new transaction backups, compiled FP64 operands, and a constant number of dense FP64 work buffers for the largest target. Backups use the original weight dtype on CPU. Snapshots copy the targeted parameters. During normal idle operation, one undo snapshot remains resident. FP32 Qwen 0.5B weights alone are roughly 2 GB; inference activations, caches, and edit workspaces add to that.

Evaluation, profiles, and match-action

The control-plane report records full WikiText-2 measurements, held-out contrastive-profile results, and real MPS request-isolation tests. The combined original ablation raised perplexity by 0.3754%. A separate formal-minus-casual direction raised it by 0.0040%. The controller gated four of twelve held-out requests: four logit distributions changed and all twelve greedy token sequences were preserved. The report includes completion-preference scores, trigger counts and generated text.

perplexity(model, token_ids, context_length, stride) computes token-weighted NLL. It scores every token except the first exactly once and returns window-level losses, counts, protocol settings, and elapsed time. The four-condition runner compares original weights, head-only ablation, MLP-only projection, and their combination on identical tokens.

ActivationProfiler(runtime, tokenizer, ActivationSite(...)) captures an input or output activation at a named module with last-token or mean-token pooling. contrast(positive, negative) returns detached CPU FP64 class means and their difference, plus source metadata. profile.operands("v_diff") feeds the compiler directly; profile.save(...) stores numeric NPZ arrays and JSON provenance. The style example uses disjoint topic sets for profiling, threshold calibration, and evaluation. It also saves a symbolic PROJECT_OUT program. Each profile records its capture location and feature space.

Rule(name, site, direction, threshold, program) defines one match-action row. MatchActionController(runtime, tokenizer, rules) uses caller-supplied rule order: the first rule with cosine_score > threshold wins. All scores are measured before any patch; identical sites share an activation capture. Rule tensors are copied on registration. Threshold calibration is a separate function operating on the designated calibration set.

controller.generate(prompt) wraps local greedy generation. For other synchronous inference engines, use controller.run(prompt, callback) or hold controller.session(prompt) for the full inference lifetime. The result separates inference time from control time, including restoration and any lock wait. These APIs serialize requests sharing one mutable model.

controller.stream(prompt, iterator_factory) keeps the scope open while consuming a synchronous iterator. Close the returned generator on early disconnect, using the same thread, for example through contextlib.closing. The controller owns cleanup of the supplied iterator. For an async server, run the entire synchronous request in a worker rather than holding a thread-owned RLock across arbitrary await points. The API runs inside the caller's Python application.
